These are my own answers, written down so that what the assistant says and what I
say in a room are the same thing.

## Why move from IT support to AI and ML engineering?

Two things, and the second one matters more.

I had been studying through the IIIT Bangalore Data Science programme alongside
the Capgemini job, finishing with the NLP specialisation in October 2025, so the
interest was two years old rather than a sudden decision.

The part that actually moved me was what I kept seeing in the queue. Problems
that took days to resolve by hand were problems a system could solve, and I
started wanting to build those systems instead of working around them. The access
request tool I built was the first time I did it, and the work felt completely
different from operating someone else's software. My dissertation is on agentic
AI and LLMs, which is the same instinct with better tools behind it.

## What ML have you actually shipped, end to end?

Nothing in a production role, and I would rather say that first than have you
find it.

What I have shipped end to end: a Python tool at Capgemini that used a language
model to turn prose access requests into concrete directory changes for my
approval, which ran daily and saved me 2 to 5 hours a week. Two analysis projects
on real datasets of 175,777 and 3,014,248 rows, with the metrics published and
the mistakes in them documented. And this assistant, which is a retrieval
pipeline with an eval harness that gates the deploy, built in the open.

That is the honest answer. The system is public, so you can check it rather than
take my word for it.

[2] Keep a human approval step between the language model and Active Directory (decision)
Access requests arrived as prose in ServiceNow tickets: create this account, add
this person to that group, revoke this permission. Reading the ticket and working
out which concrete directory change it was asking for took most of the time. The
change itself took seconds.

A language model is good at exactly that translation step, and I had an internal
one available. The question was how much authority to give it.

## Decision

The model proposes, I approve, the script applies. The model never touched the
directory directly.

## Alternatives considered

**Unattended end to end.** The script reads the ticket, decides, and makes the
change. This saves the most time and I rejected it. Directory writes are
destructive and audited, and a wrong group removal locks someone out of their job
with no clean undo. I would also have had no answer if it had gone wrong once.

**Rules and regular expressions, no model.** Fails on the actual problem. People
describe access requests in wildly inconsistent prose, and a rule set broad enough
to cover that variation becomes a worse language model.

## Consequences

It saved 2 to 5 hours a week of my own time, which was the interpretation step
rather than the approval step. I stayed accountable for every change, which was
the point.

What I did not see at the time: the approval step was a free labelled dataset. I
saw every proposal next to what I actually applied, every day, and logged none of
it. With that log I could have reported an acceptance rate, found which request
types it misread, and answered "could this run unattended?" with evidence instead
of instinct. I was shipping a model with no eval set, before I knew that was the
name for the mistake.

[3] Putting a language model in front of Active Directory access requests, with me as the approval step (case-study)
A Python tool that read the ticket, used the internal model to turn the prose into a concrete
proposed change, and then presented that proposal to me for approval. I checked it and applied
it. The model never touched the directory.

The design principle was that the model does the interpretation, which is what it is good at,
and I do the authorisation, which is what I was accountable for.

## What happened

It saved me roughly 2 to 5 hours a week. That is the interpretation and drafting step, not the
approval, which I still did on every single request.

Two things it did not do. It never gained a second user: I built it for my own queue and never
packaged it for anyone else. And it stopped running when I left the company in December 2025,
because it had exactly one owner and no handover.

## What I would do differently

**It had no owner but me, and that is a design failure, not an accident of the exit.** A tool
that saves a few hours a week is worth documenting and handing over. I never wrote down how it
worked, never sat with a colleague to get them using it, and never asked whether the team
wanted it. So the value ended on my last day, which means the honest accounting of its impact
is two and a half years of my own time and nothing beyond that.

**I did not measure how often it was right.** The approval step means I saw every proposal, so I
had a free labelled dataset sitting in front of me every day: what the model proposed against
what I actually applied. Logging that would have told me the acceptance rate, which kinds of
request it misread, and whether the gap was closing. I would then have had an evidenced answer
to "could this run unattended?" instead of an instinct. That is the same mistake as shipping a
model without an eval set, and I made it before I knew that was the name for it.

That lesson is the direct ancestor of this assistant, which measures its retrieval quality
against a golden set before anything else gets built.

[4] Putting a language model in front of Active Directory access requests, with me as the approval step (case-study)
I was handling 50 or more incidents a day in ServiceNow as a senior analyst on IT support, and
a steady share of them were access requests: an account to create, a group membership to
change, a permission to revoke. Each one was individually trivial and collectively expensive.
The work was reading a ticket written in prose, deciding what directory change it was actually
asking for, and then making that change correctly.

The slow part was not the change. It was the reading and the translating.

## Constraints

Three that shaped everything:

1. **Directory changes are destructive and auditable.** Removing the wrong group membership
   locks someone out of their job. There is no undo that leaves no trace.
2. **I had no mandate to automate anyone's work but my own.** This was a tool I built for my
   own queue, not a team initiative with a sponsor.
3. **Enterprise environment.** I could use the internal model the company provided, not an
   external API, and what I can say about the internals here is limited by the
   confidentiality terms I am still bound by. So this describes my approach and my results
   rather than their systems.

## Options I considered

**Keep doing it by hand.** The honest baseline. Reliable, and the cost was my attention rather
than any risk.

**Script it with no model.** Parse the ticket with rules and regular expressions. This fails on
the actual problem, which is that people describe access requests in wildly inconsistent prose.
A rule set that handles that variation becomes a worse version of a language model.

**Let it run unattended.** The script reads the ticket, decides, and applies the change with no
human in the loop. Fastest, and I rejected it. An LLM misreading a prose request and then
writing that misreading into a live directory is not a risk worth the minutes it saves, and I
would not have been able to defend the decision if it had gone wrong once.

[5] Leave a senior IT operations role for an MSc in AI (decision)
By 2025 I was a Senior Analyst at Capgemini, two and a half years in, running 50
or more incidents a day against SLA and administering Active Directory and
endpoint compliance across enterprise environments. The role was stable and I was
good at it.

Two things had changed underneath that. I had been studying through the IIIT
Bangalore Data Science programme alongside the job, which finished with the NLP
specialisation in October 2025, so the interest was two years old rather than
sudden. And I had built the access-request tool described in
[001](001-human-approval-before-directory-writes.md). That tool was the first
time the work felt like engineering a system rather than operating one, and I
wanted considerably more of that than the role contained.

## Decision

Resign in December 2025 and move to London for an MSc in Artificial Intelligence
and Computer Science at Northeastern University London.

## Alternatives considered

**Stay and move internally.** Capgemini is large and has ML work in it. The
honest reason I did not pursue this: internal moves from operations into
engineering are slow and usually need the credential I did not have. I would have
spent two years waiting for permission.

**Keep studying part time and stay employed.** Cheaper and lower risk, and it is
what I had already been doing for two years. It had produced certificates rather
than shipped systems, which told me the constraint was time and not motivation.

**Self-study and apply directly.** No tuition, no visa cost, no relocation. I
rejected it because I had no production ML to point at, and without either a
credential or a portfolio the applications go nowhere. The MSc buys the
credential; this assistant is meant to be the portfolio half.

[1] LR_Delivery_Time_Prediction_-Shubham-Kumar-Singh-/README.md (code)
Predicting food delivery time from the order and the state of the courier fleet at the moment
it was placed. 175,777 orders, 15 columns, from the IIIT Bangalore Data Science programme.

## Results

All figures on the held-out test set (35,156 rows).

| Model | Features | MAE (min) | RMSE | R² |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| All features | 12 | 2.33 | 3.24 | 0.8800 |
| RFE, unscaled | 8 | 2.95 | 3.98 | 0.8191 |
| RFE, scaled | 8 | 2.45 | 3.24 | 0.8737 |

**Recursive Feature Elimination made the model worse.** Dropping four features cost six points
of R². The brief framed RFE as a refinement step; on this data it was a downgrade.

The gap between the two 8-feature rows is not a scaling effect. Ordinary least squares is
scale-invariant, so standardising the inputs cannot change R². The rows differ because RFE ran
separately on each matrix and **selected different features**: the scaled run took `subtotal`
and `total_busy_dashers` where the unscaled run took `num_distinct_items` and `isWeekend`.
Swapping a weekend flag for a second courier-load count recovered five of the six lost points,
which says more about RFE's instability on correlated features than about scaling.

`distance` correlates most strongly with delivery time at r = 0.4645, with an unscaled
coefficient of 0.4803, so each additional unit adds about half a minute. Three of the eight
selected features are courier-load counts: delivery time is mostly about how busy the fleet is.

[2] Predicting delivery time with linear regression, and what feature elimination cost me (case-study)
All numbers below are on the held-out test set.

| Model | Features | MAE (min) | RMSE | R² |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| All features | 12 | 2.33 | 3.24 | 0.8800 |
| RFE, unscaled | 8 | 2.95 | 3.98 | 0.8191 |
| RFE, scaled | 8 | 2.45 | 3.24 | 0.8737 |

**Feature elimination made the model worse.** Dropping four features cost six points of R² and
half a minute of mean absolute error. I had gone in assuming the opposite, which is the useful
part: the assignment framed RFE as a refinement step, and on this data it was a downgrade.

The second row against the third is the part I would want to be asked about. Ordinary least
squares is scale-invariant, so standardising the inputs cannot change R². The two rows differ
because RFE ran on the scaled and unscaled matrices separately and **selected different
features**:

- unscaled: `market_id`, `order_protocol`, `num_distinct_items`, `total_onshift_dashers`,
  `total_outstanding_orders`, `distance`, `order_hour`, `isWeekend`
- scaled: `market_id`, `order_protocol`, `subtotal`, `total_onshift_dashers`,
  `total_busy_dashers`, `total_outstanding_orders`, `distance`, `order_hour`

Swapping `num_distinct_items` and `isWeekend` for `subtotal` and `total_busy_dashers` is what
recovered five of the six lost points. So the honest reading is not "scaling helped." It is
"RFE is unstable on correlated features, and the selection it produced on the scaled matrix
happened to be better." A second courier-load feature beat a weekend flag.

Fleet state carried real signal. Three of the eight surviving features in both runs were
courier counts, which fits the intuition that delivery time is mostly about how busy the fleet
is rather than what was ordered.

`npm install` may take a minute.

```bash
# 1. Install the dependencies
npm install

# 2. Create your environment file (holds the secret used to sign session tokens)
cp .env.example .env

# 3. Start the development server
npm run dev
```

Then open the URL printed in the terminal (by default
<http://localhost:5173>). The SQLite database file is created automatically at
`data/notes.db` the first time the app runs - there is no separate setup step.

To build and preview a production version:

```bash
npm run build
npm run preview
```

To format the source code with Prettier:

```bash
npm run format
```

## How to use

1. Open the homepage. While logged out you see generic information and links to
   **Log in** / **Register**.
2. **Register** a new account (or log in). You are taken to your homepage.
3. On the homepage, write a note with the **New note** form. Choose a category
   if you have created one.
4. Click a note's title to open the **note page**, where you can edit it,
   move it to a different category, or delete it.
5. Open **Settings** to add or remove categories.
6. Click a category (on the homepage or in Settings) to see the **category
   page** listing only that category's notes.
7. On the Settings page you can switch between a **Day** and **Night** theme.

Explain the linear regression algorithm in detail

## ✅ Answer:

**Linear Regression** is a supervised machine learning algorithm used to predict a **continuous output variable** (dependent variable) based on one or more input features (independent variables). It assumes a **linear relationship** between the inputs and the output.

---

## Types of Linear Regression

1. **Simple Linear Regression**: Uses a single input variable to predict the output.  
   Formula:  
   \[
   y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon
   \]

2. **Multiple Linear Regression**: Uses multiple input variables.  
   Formula:  
   \[
   y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \ldots + \beta_n x_n + \varepsilon
   \]

---

## ⚙️ Working Principle

- The algorithm finds the **best-fitting line** by minimizing the **Mean Squared Error (MSE)**.
- Common optimization techniques:
  - **Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)**
  - **Gradient Descent**

---

## Assumptions of Linear Regression

- Linearity between features and output
- No multicollinearity
- Homoscedasticity (constant variance)
- Normal distribution of residuals
- Independence of observations

---

## Evaluation Metrics

- **MAE**: Mean Absolute Error  
- **MSE**: Mean Squared Error  
- **RMSE**: Root Mean Squared Error  
- **R² Score**: Goodness of fit

---

---

Explain the difference between simple linear regression and multiple linear regression

## ✅ Answer:

**Simple Linear Regression** and **Multiple Linear Regression** are both types of linear regression algorithms, but they differ based on the number of input (independent) variables.

---

## Simple Linear Regression

- Involves **only one independent variable** (feature).
- It tries to fit a **straight line** to the data.
- Equation:  
  \[
  y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon
  \]  
  where:  
  - \( y \) = predicted value  
  - \( x \) = input feature  
  - \( \beta_0 \) = intercept  
  - \( \beta_1 \) = slope (coefficient)  
  - \( \varepsilon \) = error term

✅ **Use Case:** Predicting house price based on just square footage.

---

## Multiple Linear Regression

- Involves **two or more independent variables**.
- Fits a **multivariate linear equation**.
- Equation:  
  \[
  y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \ldots + \beta_n x_n + \varepsilon
  \]

✅ **Use Case:** Predicting house price based on square footage, number of bedrooms, and location score.

---

## 🔍 Key Differences

| Feature                      | Simple Linear Regression       | Multiple Linear Regression         |
|-----------------------------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| Number of Input Variables   | One                            | Two or more                         |
| Complexity                  | Low                            | Higher                              |
| Equation Type               | Single variable equation       | Multivariate equation               |
| Visualization               | 2D plot (line)                 | Multidimensional (hard to visualize)|
| Use Case                    | Simple prediction              | Complex prediction with multiple factors |

What is the role of the cost function in linear regression, and how is it minimized?

## Answer:

**Role of the Cost Function in Linear Regression:**

In linear regression, the **cost function** helps evaluate how well the model's predictions match the actual values. It measures the error between the predicted output (\( \hat{y} \)) and the actual output (\( y \)).

The most commonly used cost function in linear regression is the **Mean Squared Error (MSE)**:

\[
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
\]

Where:
- \( n \) = number of observations  
- \( y_i \) = actual value  
- \( \hat{y}_i \) = predicted value

---

## Purpose:

The goal of linear regression is to **minimize** this cost function so that the model learns the best-fitting line (or hyperplane in multiple dimensions).

---

## How is it Minimized?

To find the best coefficients \( \beta_0, \beta_1, \ldots \), we minimize the cost function using one of the following methods:

## 1. **Analytical Method (Normal Equation)**

- Direct computation using linear algebra:
\[
\beta = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y
\]
- Works well for small datasets.

## 2. **Optimization Method (Gradient Descent)**

- Iterative approach to minimize cost:
- Update rule:
\[
\beta_j = \beta_j - \alpha \cdot \frac{\partial J(\beta)}{\partial \beta_j}
\]
Where:
- \( \alpha \) = learning rate  
- \( \frac{\partial J(\beta)}{\partial \beta_j} \) = partial derivative of cost function w.r.t. parameter \( \beta_j \)

---

Predict how long a food delivery order will take, from the order itself and the state of the
courier fleet at the moment it was placed. The dataset had 175,777 orders across 15 columns:
market, order protocol, basket composition, item prices, and three fleet-state counts, with a
pickup and a delivery timestamp.

## Constraints

This was a graded assignment on the IIIT Bangalore Data Science programme, and the brief fixed
the model to linear regression. That mattered. It meant I could not answer "is a linear model
right for this?" by trying a non-linear one, so every real decision I made was about the data
and the features rather than the algorithm.

## What I did

The target did not exist in the data. I derived `time_taken` from the gap between the pickup
and delivery timestamps, then pulled `order_hour` and `isWeekend` out of the order timestamp,
and computed a `distance` feature. That gave 12 usable features.

I split 80/20 before any cleaning: 140,621 training rows and 35,156 test rows. Outliers went
next, using boxplots to see them and the interquartile range to remove them, which took the
training set from 140,621 to 139,242 rows. Just under 1%.

Then I fitted the model twice. Once on all 12 features, and once on 8 chosen by Recursive
Feature Elimination, which is the approach the brief pointed at.

whether the reranker justified its latency, and where the relevance threshold

the answer "it felt better" fails all of them.

The risk I am carrying is that the measurement work is slower and less motivating

## Update, 11 October 2026

The order did not hold. I asked for the interface first, then for working
answers, so generation came forward from Phase 5 to 9 October, and the chat box
has answered since then: from the profile, and from the passages that pass the
relevance gate. The measurement this record argued for was not dropped, only

[2] Build the eval harness before the chat interface (decision)
This assistant is a retrieval system with a chat box on the front. The chat box
is the part anyone can see and the part I most wanted to build. The retrieval
quality is the part that decides whether anything it says is true.

The phase order I am following puts corpus and ingestion first, then a retrieval
pipeline where every option is a config flag, then the eval harness, then an
ablation study across those flags, and only then the chat interface. Chat is
phase five of ten.

## Decision

No chat interface until the golden set, the retrieval metrics and the
faithfulness judge exist and produce numbers.

## Alternatives considered

**Chat first, evaluate later.** The natural order, and the one I wanted. It fails
for a specific reason rather than a moral one: once a chat UI exists, retrieval
gets tuned by asking it questions and seeing whether the answers feel right.
Feeling right is not a measurement, it does not survive a change to the chunking
strategy, and it cannot tell me whether reranking earns its latency. By the time
I built the eval harness afterwards I would be fitting it to the configuration I
had already chosen.

**Evaluate informally.** Keep a list of twenty questions and check them by hand
after changes. This is what I would actually have done, and it degrades the first
week something urgent comes up.

A Python tool that read the ticket, used the internal model to turn the prose into a concrete
proposed change, and then presented that proposal to me for approval. I checked it and applied
it. The model never touched the directory.

The design principle was that the model does the interpretation, which is what it is good at,
and I do the authorisation, which is what I was accountable for.

## What happened

It saved me roughly 2 to 5 hours a week. That is the interpretation and drafting step, not the
approval, which I still did on every single request.

Two things it did not do. It never gained a second user: I built it for my own queue and never
packaged it for anyone else. And it stopped running when I left the company in December 2025,
because it had exactly one owner and no handover.

## What I would do differently

**It had no owner but me, and that is a design failure, not an accident of the exit.** A tool
that saves a few hours a week is worth documenting and handing over. I never wrote down how it
worked, never sat with a colleague to get them using it, and never asked whether the team
wanted it. So the value ended on my last day, which means the honest accounting of its impact
is two and a half years of my own time and nothing beyond that.

**I did not measure how often it was right.** The approval step means I saw every proposal, so I
had a free labelled dataset sitting in front of me every day: what the model proposed against
what I actually applied. Logging that would have told me the acceptance rate, which kinds of
request it misread, and whether the gap was closing. I would then have had an evidenced answer
to "could this run unattended?" instead of an instinct. That is the same mistake as shipping a
model without an eval set, and I made it before I knew that was the name for it.

That lesson is the direct ancestor of this assistant, which measures its retrieval quality
against a golden set before anything else gets built.

[4] Keep a human approval step between the language model and Active Directory (decision)
Access requests arrived as prose in ServiceNow tickets: create this account, add
this person to that group, revoke this permission. Reading the ticket and working
out which concrete directory change it was asking for took most of the time. The
change itself took seconds.

A language model is good at exactly that translation step, and I had an internal
one available. The question was how much authority to give it.

## Decision

The model proposes, I approve, the script applies. The model never touched the
directory directly.

## Alternatives considered

**Unattended end to end.** The script reads the ticket, decides, and makes the
change. This saves the most time and I rejected it. Directory writes are
destructive and audited, and a wrong group removal locks someone out of their job
with no clean undo. I would also have had no answer if it had gone wrong once.

**Rules and regular expressions, no model.** Fails on the actual problem. People
describe access requests in wildly inconsistent prose, and a rule set broad enough
to cover that variation becomes a worse language model.

## Consequences

It saved 2 to 5 hours a week of my own time, which was the interpretation step
rather than the approval step. I stayed accountable for every change, which was
the point.

What I did not see at the time: the approval step was a free labelled dataset. I
saw every proposal next to what I actually applied, every day, and logged none of
it. With that log I could have reported an acceptance rate, found which request
types it misread, and answered "could this run unattended?" with evidence instead
of instinct. I was shipping a model with no eval set, before I knew that was the
name for the mistake.

set gave F1 = 0.921 ± 0.005. Oversampling duplicates minority rows before the data is
split into folds, so copies of the same claim end up in a training fold and in the fold
used to test it. The validation set was never resampled, which makes it the only honest
estimate here. The fix is to resample inside each fold.

**The simpler model won, probably because the dataset is small.** With 699 training rows
and 173 fraud cases, six significant coefficients generalised better than 200 depth-10
trees trained on 18 features.

**Part of the signal is an artefact.** `high_risk_hobby` has the largest coefficient and
comes from a leak in the data generator, so performance would likely fall a long way
without it. The validation numbers above overstate what this model would do on real
claims.

because it is negative by definition.

(994 of 999 for `insured_zip`). A model can memorise these but can't generalise from
them, so they were dropped.

`days_policy_to_incident` and `vehicle_age`, then dropped. A claim that arrives soon

**What drives retention in this data**, holding the other features fixed:
1. Seniority matters most. Senior staff have about 12 times the odds of staying of entry-level staff, and mid-level staff about 2.6 times.
2. Remote work is the clearest policy lever. Remote workers have about 5.6 times the odds of staying.
3. Work-life balance comes next. Employees who rate it Fair or Poor have roughly a third of the odds of staying of those who rate it Good or Excellent. Overtime lowers the odds too (0.72).
4. Poor or Fair company reputation and Low or Below Average performance ratings also lower the odds (0.48 to 0.72).
5. Gender, marital status and education also appear: men, married or divorced employees and PhD holders are more likely to stay. These help the model predict, but gender and marital status are sensitive characteristics, protected by employment law in many countries, so the model should not be used to treat people differently because of them. They are better read as a prompt to ask why the experience of work differs between these groups.

**Suggestions for HR:**
- Review who can work remotely, since remote workers stay far more often.
- Keep overtime in check, and follow up early on poor work-life balance scores.
- Focus retention effort on entry-level staff, for example through clearer progression to mid-level roles, because they leave the most.
- Use the model as a ranked at-risk list. In the validation data, 72.29% of the employees it flagged as likely to leave did leave.

Logistic regression on 74,610 employee records to predict who will stay at a mid-sized
technology company, and to show HR which factors go with staying.

**On 21,168 held-out employees the model recognises 74.0% of those who stayed and 73.9% of
those who left (accuracy 0.739, precision 0.755, AUC 0.825), within about half a point of
its training scores.**

## The problem

The company has mostly dealt with attrition after it happens. It wants to know in advance
who is likely to stay, who is not, and what separates the two groups, so that HR can put
retention effort where it is needed.

That asks two things of a model. It has to rank employees by their chance of staying, so HR
can start with the people least likely to stay. And it has to be explainable, because HR
needs to know what the model is reacting to before acting on it. Logistic regression gives
both: a probability for every employee, and coefficients that turn into odds ratios a
non-specialist can follow.

Stayed is the positive class throughout. Sensitivity is the share of stayers the model
recognises, and specificity is the share of leavers it recognises.

## Data

74,610 employees and 24 columns, covering demographics (age, gender, marital status,
dependents, education), the job (role, level, company size, income, tenure, promotions,
overtime, remote work, distance from home, leadership and innovation opportunities) and
ratings (work-life balance, job satisfaction, performance, company reputation,
recognition). The target is `Attrition`, Stayed or Left.

| Step | Rows | Columns |
|---|---|---|
| Raw | 74,610 | 24 |
| After dropping rows with missing values | 70,635 | 24 |
| After dropping 77 duplicate records | 70,558 | 24 |
| After dropping `Employee ID` | 70,558 | 23 |

- The data looks synthetic. 40.0% of employees would have joined before 18, Monthly Income contains placeholder values around 50,000, and Very High job satisfaction behaves like Low. The coefficients describe this dataset and may not carry over to a real workforce.
- RFE kept only dummy columns. Because a dummy's coefficient and a standardised column's coefficient are not on the same scale, numerical features such as Distance from Home (rank 3) may have been dropped too early. Testing them in the model, or using a selection method that is not based on coefficient size, is the obvious next step.

**Seniority and remote work matter most.** Holding the other features fixed, senior staff
have 12.05 times the odds of staying of entry-level staff, and mid-level staff 2.64 times.
Remote workers have 5.62 times the odds of those who do not work remotely. Remote work is
also the factor here that HR can change most directly, though the limitations below explain
why 5.62 should not be read as cause and effect.

**Work-life balance comes next.** Rating it Fair or Poor cuts the odds of staying to 0.34
and 0.29 of the Good and Excellent groups. Overtime lowers them to 0.72. A Poor or Fair view
of the company's reputation and a weak performance rating push the same way (0.48 to 0.72).

**Some strong predictors are not things HR should act on.** Single employees have 0.18
times the odds of staying of married or divorced ones, and men have 1.80 times the odds of
women. These help the model rank people, but gender and marital status are protected
characteristics in the employment law of many countries. HR can use them to ask why the
experience of work differs between groups. They should never be the basis for treating an
individual differently.

**The model holds up on new data.** Every validation measure is within about half a point of
the training figure at the same cutoff, for example accuracy 0.739 against 0.737 and AUC

overfit, and there is no sign of it.

features look like the other group's, and moving the cutoff only trades one kind of error
for the other. Getting past that would take new information about employees or a model that

At the default 0.5, sensitivity (0.754) is ahead of specificity (0.720). The curves cross
between 0.5 and 0.6, and a finer search in steps of 0.01 puts the crossing at **0.52**
(sensitivity 0.740, specificity 0.734). Accuracy hardly changes (0.738 at 0.5, 0.737 at
0.52), so moving the cutoff mostly shifts mistakes from one group to the other.

Precision and recall cross at about 0.507, close enough to 0.52 that there was no reason to
adjust it.

The crossover treats the two mistakes as equally costly: telling HR an employee is likely to
stay when they are about to leave, and flagging someone for retention effort who was going
to stay anyway. In practice the first is usually the more expensive one, since replacing a
person costs more than a conversation. With real costs the cutoff would move up, and this
curve is what you would use to move it.

model gives the stayer the higher probability about 83% of the time.

The final model is a logistic regression on the 15 features chosen by RFE. With a cutoff of 0.52, where sensitivity and specificity meet on the training data, it scores 0.7394 accuracy, 0.7397 sensitivity, 0.7391 specificity and 0.7553 precision on the validation set, with an AUC of 0.8249. These match the training figures closely, so the model generalises well to new employees.

**What drives retention in this data**, holding the other features fixed:
1. Seniority matters most. Senior staff have about 12 times the odds of staying of entry-level staff, and mid-level staff about 2.6 times.
2. Remote work is the clearest policy lever. Remote workers have about 5.6 times the odds of staying.
3. Work-life balance comes next. Employees who rate it Fair or Poor have roughly a third of the odds of staying of those who rate it Good or Excellent. Overtime lowers the odds too (0.72).

They are better read as a prompt to ask why the experience of work differs between these groups.

**Suggestions for HR:**
- Review who can work remotely, since remote workers stay far more often.
- Keep overtime in check, and follow up early on poor work-life balance scores.
- Focus retention effort on entry-level staff, for example through clearer progression to mid-level roles, because they leave the most.
- Use the model as a ranked at-risk list. In the validation data, 72.29% of the employees it flagged as likely to leave did leave.

Answering 29 questions in MySQL about India's crop insurance scheme, Pradhan Mantri Fasal
Bima Yojana (PMFBY), on 1,870 district-year records from 2018 to 2021.

## Executive summary

Madhya Pradesh (9.15 million farmers covered, summed over 2018 to 2021), Maharashtra
(8.94 million), Uttar Pradesh (7.24 million) and Rajasthan (6.82 million) account for
63.9% of all coverage. Madhya Pradesh also has the largest sum insured, ₹84,132 crore or
a quarter of the total, ahead of Rajasthan at ₹53,635 crore.

Farmers paid ₹5,624 crore of the ₹43,007 crore gross premium, or 13.1%. State governments
paid ₹19,740 crore (45.9%) and the central government ₹17,643 crore (41.0%). The farmers'
share fell every year, from 19.1% in 2018 to 10.6% in 2021, while gross premium rose from
₹7,263 crore to ₹13,119 crore.

Coverage fell from 15.0 million farmers in 2018 to 10.8 million in 2021, and the number
of reporting states dropped from 24 to 20. Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Jharkhand and
Telangana report only for 2018 and 2019, and West Bengal only for 2018. Each year, the
farmers covered equal 1.41% to 1.63% of the population of the reporting districts.
The highest state-years are Chhattisgarh in 2021 (4.97%) and Tripura in 2020 (4.68%).

Bid in Maharashtra has more farmers covered than any other district (1.43 million) and
the highest single-year farmers' premium (₹72.4 crore in 2019). Its 2019 record also has
the largest sum insured in the data. Bid, Ujjain and Latur are the only districts where
farmers paid more than ₹100 crore in total.

Karnataka's money columns look broken at source: 736,375 farmers covered against a total
sum insured of ₹3.18 lakh.

The queries behind these figures are in `summary_queries.sql`.

[2] SQL_Farmers_Insurance_Analysis/summary_queries.sql (code)
```sql
-- Queries behind the numbers in the README's executive summary. Run after setup.sql, before the solution file changes the data.

USE ndap;

-- Farmers covered per state over 2018 to 2021 (9.15, 8.94, 7.24 and 6.82 million); the fourth running share is the top-4 share (63.9%)
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    ROUND(SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) / 1000000, 2) AS farmers_covered_million,
    ROUND(100 * SUM(SUM(TotalFarmersCovered)) OVER (ORDER BY SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) DESC ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
              / SUM(SUM(TotalFarmersCovered)) OVER (), 1) AS running_share_pct
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
GROUP BY srcStateName
ORDER BY SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) DESC
LIMIT 4;

-- Largest sums insured: Madhya Pradesh (84,132 crore, a quarter of the total) and Rajasthan (53,635 crore)
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    ROUND(SUM(SumInsured) / 100) AS sum_insured_crore,
    ROUND(100 * SUM(SumInsured) / SUM(SUM(SumInsured)) OVER (), 1) AS share_of_total_pct
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
GROUP BY srcStateName
ORDER BY SUM(SumInsured) DESC
LIMIT 2;

-- Premium split: gross 43,007 crore; farmers 5,624 (13.1%), states 19,740 (45.9%), centre 17,643 crore (41.0%)
SELECT
    ROUND(SUM(GrossPremiumAmountToBePaid) / 100) AS gross_premium_crore,
    ROUND(SUM(FarmersPremiumAmount) / 100)       AS farmers_crore,
    ROUND(SUM(StatePremiumAmount) / 100)         AS states_crore,
    ROUND(SUM(GOVPremiumAmount) / 100)           AS centre_crore,
    ROUND(100 * SUM(FarmersPremiumAmount) / SUM(GrossPremiumAmountToBePaid), 1) AS farmers_pct,
    ROUND(100 * SUM(StatePremiumAmount)   / SUM(GrossPremiumAmountToBePaid), 1) AS states_pct,
    ROUND(100 * SUM(GOVPremiumAmount)     / SUM(GrossPremiumAmountToBePaid), 1) AS centre_pct
FROM FarmersInsuranceData;

-- Per year: rows (525, 505, 429, 411), states reporting (24 to 20), farmers covered (15.0 to 10.8 million),
-- gross premium (7,263 to 13,119 crore), farmers' share of premium (19.1% to 10.6%), coverage of population (1.41% to 1.63%)
SELECT
    srcYear,
    COUNT(*)                                       AS district_rows,
    COUNT(DISTINCT srcStateName)                   AS states_reporting,
    ROUND(SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) / 1000000, 1)   AS farmers_covered_million,
    ROUND(SUM(GrossPremiumAmountToBePaid) / 100)   AS gross_premium_crore,
    ROUND(100 * SUM(FarmersPremiumAmount) / SUM(GrossPremiumAmountToBePaid), 1) AS farmers_share_pct,
    ROUND(100 * SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) / SUM(TotalPopulation), 2)             AS coverage_pct_of_population
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
GROUP BY srcYear
ORDER BY srcYear;

-- States that report only some years (Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Jharkhand and Telangana 2018 and 2019; West Bengal 2018)
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT srcYear ORDER BY srcYear) AS years_reported
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
GROUP BY srcStateName
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT srcYear) < 4
ORDER BY srcStateName;

-- Highest state-years for farmers covered as a share of population (Chhattisgarh 2021 4.97%, Tripura 2020 4.68%)
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    srcYear,
    ROUND(100 * SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) / SUM(TotalPopulation), 2) AS coverage_pct_of_population
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
GROUP BY srcStateName, srcYear
ORDER BY SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) / SUM(TotalPopulation) DESC
LIMIT 2;

-- Districts with the most farmers covered (Bid first, 1.43 million)
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    srcDistrictName,
    ROUND(SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) / 1000000, 2) AS farmers_covered_million
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
GROUP BY srcStateName, srcDistrictName
ORDER BY SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) DESC
LIMIT 3;

-- The record with the highest single-year farmers' premium (Bid, 2019, 72.4 crore) also has the largest sum insured
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    srcDistrictName,
    srcYear,
    ROUND(FarmersPremiumAmount / 100, 1) AS farmers_premium_crore,
    SumInsured = (SELECT MAX(SumInsured) FROM FarmersInsuranceData) AS has_largest_sum_insured
FROM FarmersInsuranceData
WHERE FarmersPremiumAmount = (SELECT MAX(FarmersPremiumAmount) FROM FarmersInsuranceData);

HAVING SUM(FarmersPremiumAmount) > 10000

    (SELECT COUNT(*)
```

| Subqueries | Q19 to Q21 | scalar subqueries in `WHERE` and `HAVING`, nested two deep in Q21 |
| Window functions | Q22 to Q24 | `ROW_NUMBER()`, `RANK()` over grouped totals, a running `SUM()` with an explicit frame |
| Constraints | Q25 and Q26 | primary, unique and foreign keys with `ON UPDATE CASCADE` and `ON DELETE RESTRICT`, filled with `INSERT ... SELECT` |

Q12 ranks states inside each year with a window function over a grouped CTE:

```sql
WITH state_year_coverage AS (
    SELECT
        srcStateName,
        srcYear,
        100 * SUM(TotalFarmersCovered) / NULLIF(SUM(TotalPopulation), 0) AS farmers_to_population_pct
    FROM FarmersInsuranceData
    GROUP BY srcStateName, srcYear
),
ranked_states AS (
    SELECT
        srcStateName,
        srcYear,
        farmers_to_population_pct,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY srcYear ORDER BY farmers_to_population_pct DESC, srcStateName) AS rank_in_year
    FROM state_year_coverage
)
SELECT
    srcStateName,
    srcYear,
    farmers_to_population_pct,
    rank_in_year
FROM ranked_states
WHERE rank_in_year <= 3
ORDER BY farmers_to_population_pct DESC;
```

Q17 finds each district's peak premium in a grouped derived table, then joins back to the
base rows to recover the year it happened:

```sql
SELECT
    records.srcStateName,
    records.srcDistrictName,
    records.Year,
    records.TotalPopulation,
    peaks.max_farmers_premium_lakh
FROM FarmersInsuranceData AS records
INNER JOIN (
    SELECT
        srcStateName,
        srcDistrictName,
        MAX(FarmersPremiumAmount) AS max_farmers_premium_lakh
    FROM FarmersInsuranceData
    GROUP BY srcStateName, srcDistrictName
    HAVING MAX(FarmersPremiumAmount) > 2000
) AS peaks
    ON  peaks.srcStateName             = records.srcStateName
    AND peaks.srcDistrictName          = records.srcDistrictName
    AND peaks.max_farmers_premium_lakh = records.FarmersPremiumAmount
ORDER BY peaks.max_farmers_premium_lakh DESC;
```

[1] What 490,000 New York taxi trips say about when drivers actually earn (case-study)
**Tipping is about when and how, not how far.** Tip percentages are highest between 10pm and
2am, and card payments tip substantially more than cash. That is the finding I would lead
with, because it points at driver earnings rather than company revenue, and the action it
implies costs nothing: a driver choosing between a late shift and an early one has a reason to
pick the late one.

Demand moves through the day in a shape a dispatcher can use. Mornings load from the outer
residential zones into Midtown and the Financial District; evenings reverse it; late Friday and
Saturday nights concentrate in the nightlife zones; the 3am to 6am window is airport traffic
and shift workers. The top ten pickup and dropoff zones, the pickup-to-dropoff ratio per zone,
and night-hour pickup concentration are all computed directly from the trip records.

Fare per mile is not flat. Comparing vendors across three distance tiers, under 2 miles, 2 to 5,
and over 5, short trips earn far more per mile than long ones, which is what you would expect
from a fixed base fare and why long airport runs are less attractive than they look.

## What I would do differently

**Three figures in my submitted notebook are plotted from random numbers.** The starter template
seeded the zone trip counts with `np.random.randint(0, 100, len(zones))` and the route speeds
with `np.random.uniform(20, 60, ...)` as scaffolding to demonstrate the plotting calls, and I
never replaced them with real counts. A later cell then divides those random numbers by the
sampling fraction to "scale up to the full population", which scales up noise. So the trips-per-
zone choropleth and the slowest-routes analysis carry no information, and the congestion
recommendation that depended on them is withdrawn. The zone findings above come from the
value-count work, which is real. I found this on review, months after submitting, and it is the
most useful thing this project taught me: a figure that renders is not a figure that is right.

My two conclusion cells also contradict each other on peak hours, one saying 1pm to 9pm and the
other 7am to 9am and 5pm to 7pm. I did not reconcile them at the time, which means at least one
was written from impression rather than from the plot.

The conclusions themselves sit inside triple-quoted strings in code cells, so they do not render
as text. The best part of the work is nearly invisible to anyone reading the notebook.

And the recommendations need numbers. "Raise peak fares 10 to 15%" is an opinion until it comes
with an estimated revenue effect, and the data could have supported that estimate. A
recommendation without a number is not an analysis result.

Finally, I would test whether the filtering shaped the findings. Removing trips over 180 minutes
and over 50 miles is defensible, but those are exactly the trips that matter most to a driver
deciding whether to take an airport run. I should have run the headline findings once with the
bounds and once without and reported whether they held.

worse and I did not notice at the time, because I treated RFE as a step you apply

count. The lesson I took is that a result needs an explanation before it is a
result, and I had an unexplained six-point gap sitting in my notebook for a year.

**The random forest overfits.** It scores 1.000 on every training metric before tuning
and 0.982 accuracy after, then drops to 0.813 accuracy and F1 0.659 on validation, below
the logistic regression on all six measures. Grid search chose `max_depth=10` and
`min_samples_leaf=1` (the grid also offered depths of 6 and unlimited, and leaf sizes of
3 and 5), and trees that size still fit the oversampled training set almost perfectly.

**The cross-validated scores are inflated.** Cross-validation on the oversampled training
set gave F1 = 0.921 ± 0.005. Oversampling duplicates minority rows before the data is
split into folds, so copies of the same claim end up in a training fold and in the fold
used to test it. The validation set was never resampled, which makes it the only honest
estimate here. The fix is to resample inside each fold.

**The simpler model won, probably because the dataset is small.** With 699 training rows
and 173 fraud cases, six significant coefficients generalised better than 200 depth-10
trees trained on 18 features.

**Part of the signal is an artefact.** `high_risk_hobby` has the largest coefficient and
comes from a leak in the data generator, so performance would likely fall a long way
without it. The validation numbers above overstate what this model would do on real
claims.

AI and LLMs, which is the same instinct with better tools behind it.

## What ML have you actually shipped, end to end?

Nothing in a production role, and I would rather say that first than have you
find it.

What I have shipped end to end: a Python tool at Capgemini that used a language
model to turn prose access requests into concrete directory changes for my
approval, which ran daily and saved me 2 to 5 hours a week. Two analysis projects
on real datasets of 175,777 and 3,014,248 rows, with the metrics published and
the mistakes in them documented. And this assistant, which is a retrieval
pipeline with an eval harness that gates the deploy, built in the open.

take my word for it.

[2] Putting a language model in front of Active Directory access requests, with me as the approval step (case-study)
A Python tool that read the ticket, used the internal model to turn the prose into a concrete
proposed change, and then presented that proposal to me for approval. I checked it and applied
it. The model never touched the directory.

The design principle was that the model does the interpretation, which is what it is good at,
and I do the authorisation, which is what I was accountable for.

## What happened

It saved me roughly 2 to 5 hours a week. That is the interpretation and drafting step, not the
approval, which I still did on every single request.

Two things it did not do. It never gained a second user: I built it for my own queue and never
packaged it for anyone else. And it stopped running when I left the company in December 2025,
because it had exactly one owner and no handover.

## What I would do differently

**It had no owner but me, and that is a design failure, not an accident of the exit.** A tool
that saves a few hours a week is worth documenting and handing over. I never wrote down how it
worked, never sat with a colleague to get them using it, and never asked whether the team
wanted it. So the value ended on my last day, which means the honest accounting of its impact
is two and a half years of my own time and nothing beyond that.

**I did not measure how often it was right.** The approval step means I saw every proposal, so I
had a free labelled dataset sitting in front of me every day: what the model proposed against
what I actually applied. Logging that would have told me the acceptance rate, which kinds of
request it misread, and whether the gap was closing. I would then have had an evidenced answer
to "could this run unattended?" instead of an instinct. That is the same mistake as shipping a
model without an eval set, and I made it before I knew that was the name for it.

That lesson is the direct ancestor of this assistant, which measures its retrieval quality
against a golden set before anything else gets built.

[3] Keep a human approval step between the language model and Active Directory (decision)
Access requests arrived as prose in ServiceNow tickets: create this account, add
this person to that group, revoke this permission. Reading the ticket and working
out which concrete directory change it was asking for took most of the time. The
change itself took seconds.

A language model is good at exactly that translation step, and I had an internal
one available. The question was how much authority to give it.

## Decision

The model proposes, I approve, the script applies. The model never touched the
directory directly.

## Alternatives considered

**Unattended end to end.** The script reads the ticket, decides, and makes the
change. This saves the most time and I rejected it. Directory writes are
destructive and audited, and a wrong group removal locks someone out of their job
with no clean undo. I would also have had no answer if it had gone wrong once.

**Rules and regular expressions, no model.** Fails on the actual problem. People
describe access requests in wildly inconsistent prose, and a rule set broad enough
to cover that variation becomes a worse language model.

## Consequences

It saved 2 to 5 hours a week of my own time, which was the interpretation step
rather than the approval step. I stayed accountable for every change, which was
the point.

What I did not see at the time: the approval step was a free labelled dataset. I
saw every proposal next to what I actually applied, every day, and logged none of
it. With that log I could have reported an acceptance rate, found which request
types it misread, and answered "could this run unattended?" with evidence instead
of instinct. I was shipping a model with no eval set, before I knew that was the
name for the mistake.

**The random forest overfits.** It scores 1.000 on every training metric before tuning
and 0.982 accuracy after, then drops to 0.813 accuracy and F1 0.659 on validation, below
the logistic regression on all six measures. Grid search chose `max_depth=10` and
`min_samples_leaf=1` (the grid also offered depths of 6 and unlimited, and leaf sizes of
3 and 5), and trees that size still fit the oversampled training set almost perfectly.

**The cross-validated scores are inflated.** Cross-validation on the oversampled training
set gave F1 = 0.921 ± 0.005. Oversampling duplicates minority rows before the data is
split into folds, so copies of the same claim end up in a training fold and in the fold
used to test it. The validation set was never resampled, which makes it the only honest
estimate here. The fix is to resample inside each fold.

**The simpler model won, probably because the dataset is small.** With 699 training rows
and 173 fraud cases, six significant coefficients generalised better than 200 depth-10
trees trained on 18 features.

**Part of the signal is an artefact.** `high_risk_hobby` has the largest coefficient and
comes from a leak in the data generator, so performance would likely fall a long way
without it. The validation numbers above overstate what this model would do on real
claims.

I was handling 50 or more incidents a day in ServiceNow as a senior analyst on IT support, and
a steady share of them were access requests: an account to create, a group membership to
change, a permission to revoke. Each one was individually trivial and collectively expensive.
The work was reading a ticket written in prose, deciding what directory change it was actually
asking for, and then making that change correctly.

The slow part was not the change. It was the reading and the translating.

## Constraints

Three that shaped everything:

1. **Directory changes are destructive and auditable.** Removing the wrong group membership
   locks someone out of their job. There is no undo that leaves no trace.
2. **I had no mandate to automate anyone's work but my own.** This was a tool I built for my
   own queue, not a team initiative with a sponsor.
3. **Enterprise environment.** I could use the internal model the company provided, not an
   external API, and what I can say about the internals here is limited by the
   confidentiality terms I am still bound by. So this describes my approach and my results
   rather than their systems.

## Options I considered

**Keep doing it by hand.** The honest baseline. Reliable, and the cost was my attention rather
than any risk.

**Script it with no model.** Parse the ticket with rules and regular expressions. This fails on
the actual problem, which is that people describe access requests in wildly inconsistent prose.
A rule set that handles that variation becomes a worse version of a language model.

**Let it run unattended.** The script reads the ticket, decides, and applies the change with no
human in the loop. Fastest, and I rejected it. An LLM misreading a prose request and then
writing that misreading into a live directory is not a risk worth the minutes it saves, and I
would not have been able to defend the decision if it had gone wrong once.

[2] Keep a human approval step between the language model and Active Directory (decision)
Access requests arrived as prose in ServiceNow tickets: create this account, add
this person to that group, revoke this permission. Reading the ticket and working
out which concrete directory change it was asking for took most of the time. The
change itself took seconds.

A language model is good at exactly that translation step, and I had an internal
one available. The question was how much authority to give it.

## Decision

The model proposes, I approve, the script applies. The model never touched the
directory directly.

## Alternatives considered

**Unattended end to end.** The script reads the ticket, decides, and makes the
change. This saves the most time and I rejected it. Directory writes are
destructive and audited, and a wrong group removal locks someone out of their job
with no clean undo. I would also have had no answer if it had gone wrong once.

**Rules and regular expressions, no model.** Fails on the actual problem. People
describe access requests in wildly inconsistent prose, and a rule set broad enough
to cover that variation becomes a worse language model.

## Consequences

It saved 2 to 5 hours a week of my own time, which was the interpretation step
rather than the approval step. I stayed accountable for every change, which was
the point.

What I did not see at the time: the approval step was a free labelled dataset. I
saw every proposal next to what I actually applied, every day, and logged none of
it. With that log I could have reported an acceptance rate, found which request
types it misread, and answered "could this run unattended?" with evidence instead
of instinct. I was shipping a model with no eval set, before I knew that was the
name for the mistake.

[3] Putting a language model in front of Active Directory access requests, with me as the approval step (case-study)
A Python tool that read the ticket, used the internal model to turn the prose into a concrete
proposed change, and then presented that proposal to me for approval. I checked it and applied
it. The model never touched the directory.

The design principle was that the model does the interpretation, which is what it is good at,
and I do the authorisation, which is what I was accountable for.

## What happened

It saved me roughly 2 to 5 hours a week. That is the interpretation and drafting step, not the
approval, which I still did on every single request.

Two things it did not do. It never gained a second user: I built it for my own queue and never
packaged it for anyone else. And it stopped running when I left the company in December 2025,
because it had exactly one owner and no handover.

## What I would do differently

**It had no owner but me, and that is a design failure, not an accident of the exit.** A tool
that saves a few hours a week is worth documenting and handing over. I never wrote down how it
worked, never sat with a colleague to get them using it, and never asked whether the team
wanted it. So the value ended on my last day, which means the honest accounting of its impact
is two and a half years of my own time and nothing beyond that.

**I did not measure how often it was right.** The approval step means I saw every proposal, so I
had a free labelled dataset sitting in front of me every day: what the model proposed against
what I actually applied. Logging that would have told me the acceptance rate, which kinds of
request it misread, and whether the gap was closing. I would then have had an evidenced answer
to "could this run unattended?" instead of an instinct. That is the same mistake as shipping a
model without an eval set, and I made it before I knew that was the name for it.

That lesson is the direct ancestor of this assistant, which measures its retrieval quality
against a golden set before anything else gets built.

[1] Fraudulent_Claim_Detection/README.md (code)
Classifying auto insurance claims as fraudulent or legitimate using logistic regression
and random forest, on 1,000 historical claims with a 24.7% fraud rate.

**On held-out claims, logistic regression catches 84% of frauds at 85% specificity
(F1 0.729, AUC 0.855). It beats a tuned random forest on every validation metric, even
though the forest scores 0.982 accuracy on the training set (1.000 before tuning).**

## The problem

An insurer reviewing motor claims has two ways to lose money. Paying a fraudulent claim
costs the payout. Investigating an honest one costs an adjuster's time and irritates a
customer who did nothing wrong. Reviewing every claim is not affordable, so the question
is which claims to look at.

The model's first job is therefore to rank claims by risk, so a small review team can
start at the top. Picking the cutoff on that ranking comes second.

## Data

1,000 claims, 40 columns, covering policy details, the insured party, the incident, and
claim amounts. Target is `fraud_reported` (Y/N), 24.7% positive.

| Step | Rows | Columns |
|---|---|---|
| Raw | 1,000 | 40 |
| After dropping `_c39` (entirely empty) | 1,000 | 39 |
| After dropping one invalid row | 999 | 39 |
| After dropping identifiers, adding derived features | 999 | 35 |
| Train / validation (70/30, stratified) | 699 / 300 | 34 |

[2] Fraudulent_Claim_Detection/Fraudulent_Claim_Detection_Shubham_Kumar_Singh.ipynb (code)
My final model is the 6-feature logistic regression with a cutoff of 0.60. On the validation set, which keeps the natural fraud rate, it caught 62 of the 74 fraudulent claims, with sensitivity 0.838, specificity 0.850, precision 0.646, F1 0.729 and AUC 0.855.

The tuned random forest overfitted. It scored 0.982 accuracy on the training data but did worse than the logistic regression on every validation metric (F1 0.659, AUC 0.825). Its cross-validated F1 of 0.926 was also too optimistic, because I oversampled before cross-validation and copies of the same fraud claims ended up in both training and test folds. The validation set was never resampled, so its numbers are the ones I trust.

Most of the signal comes from incident severity and the high-risk hobby flag. Incident severity and insured hobbies had the two biggest spreads in fraud rate in the EDA, and in the final model the hobby flag and the three severity levels have the four largest coefficients. Severity makes sense, since Major Damage claims were fraudulent 60.9% of the time. The hobby flag does not: there is no real reason chess and cross-fit players would have fraud rates of 90.6% and 76.0%, so I think it is an artefact of the synthetic data and would not carry over to real claims.

The 0.60 cutoff treats a missed fraud and a false alarm as equally costly, which is not true for an insurer. The next step would be to set the cutoff from the real cost of each type of error, and to move the oversampling inside each cross-validation fold.

[3] Fraudulent_Claim_Detection/README.md (code)
**The random forest overfits.** It scores 1.000 on every training metric before tuning
and 0.982 accuracy after, then drops to 0.813 accuracy and F1 0.659 on validation, below
the logistic regression on all six measures. Grid search chose `max_depth=10` and
`min_samples_leaf=1` (the grid also offered depths of 6 and unlimited, and leaf sizes of
3 and 5), and trees that size still fit the oversampled training set almost perfectly.

**The cross-validated scores are inflated.** Cross-validation on the oversampled training
set gave F1 = 0.921 ± 0.005. Oversampling duplicates minority rows before the data is
split into folds, so copies of the same claim end up in a training fold and in the fold
used to test it. The validation set was never resampled, which makes it the only honest
estimate here. The fix is to resample inside each fold.

**The simpler model won, probably because the dataset is small.** With 699 training rows
and 173 fraud cases, six significant coefficients generalised better than 200 depth-10
trees trained on 18 features.

**Part of the signal is an artefact.** `high_risk_hobby` has the largest coefficient and
comes from a leak in the data generator, so performance would likely fall a long way
without it. The validation numbers above overstate what this model would do on real
claims.

## Class balance

![Class balance](images/class-balance.png)

24.7% of claims are fraudulent. That is enough imbalance to make accuracy misleading:
predicting "not fraud" for every claim scores 75.3% and catches nothing.

The training set was oversampled to 50/50 with `RandomOverSampler`, taking it from 699
to 1,052 rows. The validation set was left at its natural rate, because a metric measured
on a balanced set would not describe how the model behaves on real claim traffic.

## Feature selection

85 columns after one-hot encoding. RFECV with F1 scoring selected 6.

RFECV picks features by predictive score and ignores p-values, so I checked its picks in
statsmodels: drop the least significant feature if its p-value is above 0.05, refit, and
repeat, then do the same for any VIF above 5. Going one feature at a time matters because
each p-value depends on the other features in the model.

None needed removing. The final model has 6 features, a maximum p-value of 0.0463 and a
maximum VIF of 1.20: the hobby flag, three incident-severity levels (Total Loss, Minor
Damage and Trivial Damage, with Major Damage as the baseline), the handlers-cleaners
occupation and a grouped "other" car make.
